messages.subject: trajectory analysis with "non-independent" population pairs
parts:
Dear all, 

I have a couple of geomorph-specific (but probably also more statistical/conceptual) questions regarding measuring the extent of parallel phenotypic evolution. 

Briefly, I have data for eight fish populations. Two of those are from very large lakes (let's call them Source1 and Source2), which have acted as source for the other six small populations (Derived1 - Derived6). 
One of the small lakes (Derived1) has been colonized from Source1, whereas the other five (Derived2 - 6) have been colonized from Source2. 

My main aim is to quantify the extent (amount and direction) of phenotypic change of all small lake populations, but I ran into some problems given the "non-independence" of my population pairs. 

First, I was thinking about analyzing this using the trajectory.analysis function, but my data does not seem to fit the generic input data format as one and the same population (Source2) would have to be assigned to several pairs (unless I missed something obvious). 
I can get the function running by duplicating individuals from Source2 several times and assigning them to five "independent" pairs. The output seems to make sense, but I am not sure about the effects of this. A plot of the first two axes of a PCA with and without the duplicated individuals (independent GPAs) looks almost identical and the PC axes explain an almost identical amount of variation. Thus, I am tempted to conclude that duplicating these individuals did not have a strong effect and given some caveats I can use this approach. Yet, I am wondering what people with more experience and a stronger statistical background think. Is this procedure justifiable? 

I also performed all five possible independent analyses (Source1Derived1 / Source2Derived2, Source1Derived1 / Source2Derived3, etc.), but since the results are then derived from independent GPAs and PCAs I assume I cannot properly compare the five small lakes (e.g. even qualitatively saying Source2Derived2 is parallel to Source1Derived1, so if Source2Derived3 is not parallel to Source1Derived1, then Source2Derived2 and Source2Derived3 don't show a lot parallelism ). Is that correct? One cannot compare trajectories from independent analyses (even though one population pair is always the same). 

Alternatively, I thought about using advanced.procD.lm similar to what has been described in a recent post here, however I would be interested in the difference in lengths and angles among all pairs and I am not sure how to do this (get the angles). Also, is there a convenient way to plot the vectors in 2D-space (analogous to a plot of the TA)? 

Any comments or suggestions on my thoughts and how I should proceed would be very much appreciated. 

Thanks, 
Andi

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] trajectory analysis with "non-independent" population pairs
parts:
Andy,

I think the best way to go about this is a two-pronged approach.  Your instincts for trajectory analysis were good, but as you have found out, that is a function for a factorial model.  But yes, you can do something similar with advanced.procD.lm.

First prong, I would use procD.lm to see if pairwise tests are warranted.

fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ derived/source, …)

This will have to be updated for nested effects.

fit <- update.nested(fit, ~derived/source)
summary(fit)

If the derived effect is not significant, you can stop here.  If significant, I think this should work as the second prong:

fit2 <- advanced.procD.lm(Y ~ derived/source, ~ source, groups = ~derived, ...)

summary(fit2)

This approach assumes - as you have suggested - that the original sources 1 and 2 are levels represented in your variable, derived.  The approach above will allow you to test if the vectors between least squares means are significantly longer than expected by chance, holding constant the variation between source populations.  Thus, any source-derived value that is significant means the new populations have significantly diverged in terms of the magnitude of phenotypic change.  You could also create vectors of phenotypic change like in the post you linked.  Either way should work.

To ascertain if the derived populations changed in different directions is a bit trickier.  You would have to create the vectors like in the post you linked, but calculate either the vector correlation or angle between vectors for every random permutation.  We currently do not have all the random means as output, just because it normally would be cumbersome.  We could update that, and then you would have to figure out how to calculate all vector correlations or angles between different vectors, in every permutation.  Just as easily (relatively speaking), one could write a routine that does advanced.procD.lm with 1 iteration many times in a (randomization) loop and extract the LS means each time.  Regardless, the intent here is to recreate what trajectory analysis does, when one does not have a factorial model.

Finally, one bit of output from advanced.procD.lm is the LS means.  Save these and do a PCA; e.g., 

myMeans <- fit2$LS.means
PCA <- prcomp(myMeans)
P <- Y%*%PCA$rotation # project data onto between-group PC axes
Pm <- myMeans%*%PCA$rotation # project means onto between-group PC axes
plot(P[,1:2], cex=0.5, …) # plot rotated data space, add color to points if desired
points(Pm[,1:2], cex=1.5, …) # add big points for means; now you have something similar to trajectory plot

If you do not do the direction test, this plot might help inform if the direction of phenotypic change was consistent.

Hope this was helpful!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] trajectory analysis with "non-independent" population pairs
parts:
Mike, 

Thank you so much for your fast and very elaborate reply! That was really helpful. 

I'm afraid I still have some questions, though. 

1.) I am a bit confused about the variables in your example. You wrote that "...the original sources 1 and 2 are levels represented in your variable, derived". So, in your example "derived" would only have two levels (Source1 and Source2) and "source" would specify the individual lakes. Is that correct? Sorry, just regarding the variable names I would think it should the other way around and this may have been a typo, but like this it does makes sense for the nested model in your example (Y ~ derived/source -> lakes are nested within source populations as they are replicates of colonization and evolution). I would think that I need one variable "lake" with eight levels that is nested within the "source" variable that has two levels only. The model would then be (coords ~ source/lakes). Does that make sense? How would I deal with the actual source populations? Simply assign them as their own source populations? 

2.) I have to ask: given that the trajectory analysis is so straightforward, I would definitely prefer it over a potentially error-prone manual approach or not quantifying the angles at all. Is performing a TA with duplicated data a categorical no-go or can that be justified? I know that's a tricky question (how wrong is too wrong), but given that the PCAs with and without the duplicates appear almost identical I was wondering if this would be a justifiable workaround. Potentially in support of this, I did project the LS means onto the between-group PCA - as you suggested, thanks again! - (with a -hopefully sensible- model using lakes nested within source as described above) and if I draw vectors between derived lake populations and their sources it looks almost identical to the trajectory.analysis plot I got before with duplicated individuals. 

I would be very grateful for your help. 

Cheers, 
Andi
